claim: The most lethal form of malaria in humans is caused by Plasmodium falciparum.
source: The most lethal form of malaria in humans is caused by Plasmodium falciparum.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about malaria.

claim: Plasmodium falciparum parasites invade erythrocytes through a complex process involving multiple ligand-receptor interactions.
source: These parasites invade erythrocytes, a complex process involving multiple ligand-receptor interactions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about P. falciparum invasion mechanisms.

claim: EBA-175 mediates substantial changes in the deformability of erythrocytes by binding to glycophorin A.
source: We show EBA-175 mediates substantial changes in the deformability of erythrocytes by binding to glycophorin A and activating a phosphorylation cascade that includes erythrocyte cytoskeletal proteins resulting in changes in the viscoelastic properties of the host cell.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including AFM measurements and rheology experiments.

claim: EBA-175 binding to glycophorin A activates a phosphorylation cascade that includes erythrocyte cytoskeletal proteins.
source: We show EBA-175 mediates substantial changes in the deformability of erythrocytes by binding to glycophorin A and activating a phosphorylation cascade that includes erythrocyte cytoskeletal proteins resulting in changes in the viscoelastic properties of the host cell.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data showing phosphorylation of cytoskeletal proteins.

claim: TRPM7 kinase inhibitors FTY720 and waixenicin A block the changes in the deformability of erythrocytes.
source: TRPM7 kinase inhibitors FTY720 and waixenicin A block the changes in the deformability of erythrocytes and inhibit merozoite invasion by directly inhibiting the phosphorylation cascade.
evidence: This is supported by AFM measurements and invasion assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: FTY720 and waixenicin A inhibit merozoite invasion by directly inhibiting the phosphorylation cascade.
source: TRPM7 kinase inhibitors FTY720 and waixenicin A block the changes in the deformability of erythrocytes and inhibit merozoite invasion by directly inhibiting the phosphorylation cascade.
evidence: This is supported by invasion inhibition assays and phosphoproteomics data.

claim: Binding of P. falciparum parasites to the erythrocyte directly activates a signaling pathway through a phosphorylation cascade.
source: Therefore, binding of P. falciparum parasites to the erythrocyte directly activate a signaling pathway through a phosphorylation cascade and this alters the viscoelastic properties of the host membrane conditioning it for successful invasion.
evidence: This is supported by phosphoproteomics data showing increased phosphorylation upon ligand binding.

claim: The phosphorylation cascade alters the viscoelastic properties of the host membrane conditioning it for successful invasion.
source: Therefore, binding of P. falciparum parasites to the erythrocyte directly activate a signaling pathway through a phosphorylation cascade and this alters the viscoelastic properties of the host membrane conditioning it for successful invasion.
evidence: This is supported by AFM measurements, rheology data, and invasion assays.

claim: Merozoite invasion involves dramatic changes including deformation of the erythrocyte.
source: Attachment and internalization involve a series of dramatic changes that include deformation of the erythrocyte (Figure 1A) and calcium (Ca2+) influx after which a tight junction is formed and invasion mediated using force generated by the parasite actomyosin motor (Weiss et al., 2015; Volz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by live imaging data (Figure 1A) and citations to previous work.

claim: Merozoite invasion involves calcium (Ca2+) influx.
source: Attachment and internalization involve a series of dramatic changes that include deformation of the erythrocyte (Figure 1A) and calcium (Ca2+) influx after which a tight junction is formed and invasion mediated using force generated by the parasite actomyosin motor (Weiss et al., 2015; Volz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A tight junction is formed after erythrocyte deformation and calcium influx during merozoite invasion.
source: Attachment and internalization involve a series of dramatic changes that include deformation of the erythrocyte (Figure 1A) and calcium (Ca2+) influx after which a tight junction is formed and invasion mediated using force generated by the parasite actomyosin motor (Weiss et al., 2015; Volz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Invasion is mediated using force generated by the parasite actomyosin motor.
source: Attachment and internalization involve a series of dramatic changes that include deformation of the erythrocyte (Figure 1A) and calcium (Ca2+) influx after which a tight junction is formed and invasion mediated using force generated by the parasite actomyosin motor (Weiss et al., 2015; Volz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The mechanical alterations of the erythrocyte that occur during merozoite invasion have been described using video-microscopy.
source: The mechanical alterations of the erythrocyte that occur during merozoite invasion have been described using video-microscopy (Weiss et al., 2015; Gilson et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Merozoite invasion involves the interaction of multiple parasite ligands with specific erythrocyte receptors including MSPs, EBAs, and PfRhs.
source: Merozoite invasion involves the interaction of multiple parasite ligands with specific erythrocyte receptors that include merozoite surface proteins (MSPs) (Hodder et al., 2012), erythrocyte binding antigens (EBAs) (Adams et al., 2001) and reticulocyte binding-like homologs (PfRhs) (Rayner et al., 2000; Triglia et al., 2001; Hayton et al., 2008; Baum et al., 2009), and the functional requirement of these during specific steps of the invasion has been defined (Weiss et al., 2015; Volz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: MSPDBL1 and MSPDBL2 bind to unknown receptors.
source: This includes binding of the merozoite surface protein Duffy Binding-Like 1 and 2 (MSPDBL1 and 2) with unknown receptors (Hodder et al., 2010), EBA-175 with glycophorin A (GPA) (Orlandi et al., 1992), EBA-140 (also known as BAEBL) with glycophorin C (GPC) (Maier et al., 2003), PfRh4 with Complement Receptor 1 (CR1) (Tham et al., 2010) and PfRh5 with basigin (Crosnier et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: EBA-175 binds to glycophorin A (GPA).
source: This includes binding of the merozoite surface protein Duffy Binding-Like 1 and 2 (MSPDBL1 and 2) with unknown receptors (Hodder et al., 2010), EBA-175 with glycophorin A (GPA) (Orlandi et al., 1992), EBA-140 (also known as BAEBL) with glycophorin C (GPC) (Maier et al., 2003), PfRh4 with Complement Receptor 1 (CR1) (Tham et al., 2010) and PfRh5 with basigin (Crosnier et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: EBA-140 (also known as BAEBL) binds to glycophorin C (GPC).
source: This includes binding of the merozoite surface protein Duffy Binding-Like 1 and 2 (MSPDBL1 and 2) with unknown receptors (Hodder et al., 2010), EBA-175 with glycophorin A (GPA) (Orlandi et al., 1992), EBA-140 (also known as BAEBL) with glycophorin C (GPC) (Maier et al., 2003), PfRh4 with Complement Receptor 1 (CR1) (Tham et al., 2010) and PfRh5 with basigin (Crosnier et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: PfRh4 binds to Complement Receptor 1 (CR1).
source: This includes binding of the merozoite surface protein Duffy Binding-Like 1 and 2 (MSPDBL1 and 2) with unknown receptors (Hodder et al., 2010), EBA-175 with glycophorin A (GPA) (Orlandi et al., 1992), EBA-140 (also known as BAEBL) with glycophorin C (GPC) (Maier et al., 2003), PfRh4 with Complement Receptor 1 (CR1) (Tham et al., 2010) and PfRh5 with basigin (Crosnier et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: PfRh5 binds to basigin.
source: This includes binding of the merozoite surface protein Duffy Binding-Like 1 and 2 (MSPDBL1 and 2) with unknown receptors (Hodder et al., 2010), EBA-175 with glycophorin A (GPA) (Orlandi et al., 1992), EBA-140 (also known as BAEBL) with glycophorin C (GPC) (Maier et al., 2003), PfRh4 with Complement Receptor 1 (CR1) (Tham et al., 2010) and PfRh5 with basigin (Crosnier et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Nothing is known with respect to alterations that ligand-receptor interactions mediate on the host cell during initial stages of merozoite invasion.
source: Nothing is known with respect to alterations that these ligand-receptor interactions mediate on the host cell during these initial stages of merozoite invasion.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge prior to this study.

claim: Erythrocytes are very flexible and dynamic cells that are able to flow smoothly through the microvasculature and pass swiftly through the spleen.
source: Erythrocytes are very flexible and dynamic cells that are able to flow smoothly through the microvasculature and pass swiftly through the spleen.
evidence: This is established knowledge about erythrocyte properties.

claim: The shear elastic properties of the erythrocyte are predominantly determined by the underlying spectrin network and the connection of integral membrane proteins with this cytoskeleton.
source: The shear elastic properties of the erythrocyte are predominantly determined by the underlying spectrin network as well as the connection of integral membrane proteins with this cytoskeleton.
evidence: This is established knowledge about erythrocyte structure and mechanics.

claim: The erythrocyte can undergo repeated large deformations to facilitate movement through microcapillaries.
source: The erythrocyte can undergo repeated large deformations to facilitate movement through microcapillaries, and these deformations involve the dynamic remodeling of the spectrin network (Li et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Erythrocyte deformations involve the dynamic remodeling of the spectrin network.
source: The erythrocyte can undergo repeated large deformations to facilitate movement through microcapillaries, and these deformations involve the dynamic remodeling of the spectrin network (Li et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Under normal physiological conditions, calcium (Ca2+) influx or treatment with certain amphipathic drugs can induce membrane budding.
source: Additionally, under normal physiological conditions, calcium (Ca2+) influx or treatment with certain amphipathic drugs can induce membrane budding (Zuccala et al., 2011; Allan et al., 1976; Ben-Bassat et al., 1972).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Active ATP-dependent cytoskeleton forces that are uncorrelated with Brownian noise have been detected in erythrocytes.
source: Also, active ATP-dependent cytoskeleton forces that are uncorrelated with Brownian noise have been detected in erythrocytes (Rodríguez-García et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Environmental factors can trigger post-translational modifications and change the erythrocyte membrane properties.
source: Environmental factors can trigger post-translational modifications and change the erythrocyte membrane properties, and antibody ligation of CR1 increases erythrocyte membrane deformability (Glodek et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Antibody ligation of CR1 increases erythrocyte membrane deformability.
source: Environmental factors can trigger post-translational modifications and change the erythrocyte membrane properties, and antibody ligation of CR1 increases erythrocyte membrane deformability (Glodek et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Phosphorylation and dephosphorylation of membrane and cytoskeletal proteins is a likely mechanism by which properties of the erythrocyte membrane are regulated.
source: Phosphorylation and dephosphorylation of membrane and cytoskeletal proteins is a likely mechanism by which properties of the erythrocyte membrane are regulated (Mohandas and Gallagher, 2008), and increased phosphorylation of erythrocyte proteins occurs on attachment of P. falciparum merozoites suggesting changes to the host cell cytoskeleton may be important for parasite entry (Zuccala et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Increased phosphorylation of erythrocyte proteins occurs on attachment of P. falciparum merozoites.
source: Phosphorylation and dephosphorylation of membrane and cytoskeletal proteins is a likely mechanism by which properties of the erythrocyte membrane are regulated (Mohandas and Gallagher, 2008), and increased phosphorylation of erythrocyte proteins occurs on attachment of P. falciparum merozoites suggesting changes to the host cell cytoskeleton may be important for parasite entry (Zuccala et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Changes to the host cell cytoskeleton may be important for parasite entry.
source: Phosphorylation and dephosphorylation of membrane and cytoskeletal proteins is a likely mechanism by which properties of the erythrocyte membrane are regulated (Mohandas and Gallagher, 2008), and increased phosphorylation of erythrocyte proteins occurs on attachment of P. falciparum merozoites suggesting changes to the host cell cytoskeleton may be important for parasite entry (Zuccala et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work and represents speculation about the importance of cytoskeletal changes.

claim: Erythrocyte stiffness was generally reduced by binding of MSPDBL1, MSPDBL2, PfRh4, PfRh5 and EBA-140 RII (p<0.0001).
source: Erythrocyte stiffness was generally reduced by binding of MSPDBL1, MSPDBL2, PfRh4, PfRh5 and EBA-140 RII (p<0.0001) with EBA-175 RII binding showing a dramatic reduction of Young's modulus (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by AFM data shown in Figure 1B and supplementary figures.

claim: EBA-175 RII binding showed a dramatic reduction of Young's modulus.
source: Erythrocyte stiffness was generally reduced by binding of MSPDBL1, MSPDBL2, PfRh4, PfRh5 and EBA-140 RII (p<0.0001) with EBA-175 RII binding showing a dramatic reduction of Young's modulus (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by AFM data shown in Figure 1B and supplementary figures.

claim: The erythrocyte-binding domain of EBA-175 is region II, a 616 amino acid fragment consisting of two cysteine-rich Duffy binding-like (DBL) domains (F1 and F2).
source: The erythrocyte-binding domain of EBA-175 is region II, a 616 amino acid fragment consisting of two cysteine-rich Duffy binding-like (DBL) domains (F1 and F2) (Tolia et al., 2005), that binds GPA (Figure 1C) (Sim et al., 1994; Salinas et al., 2014; Salinas and Tolia, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: EBA-175 region II binds GPA.
source: The erythrocyte-binding domain of EBA-175 is region II, a 616 amino acid fragment consisting of two cysteine-rich Duffy binding-like (DBL) domains (F1 and F2) (Tolia et al., 2005), that binds GPA (Figure 1C) (Sim et al., 1994; Salinas et al., 2014; Salinas and Tolia, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: EBA-175 dimerizes upon receptor engagement.
source: EBA-175 dimerizes upon receptor engagement (Tolia et al., 2005), and neutralizing antibodies block the dimer interface and receptor binding residues of EBA-175 RII (Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Neutralizing antibodies block the dimer interface and receptor binding residues of EBA-175 RII.
source: EBA-175 dimerizes upon receptor engagement (Tolia et al., 2005), and neutralizing antibodies block the dimer interface and receptor binding residues of EBA-175 RII (Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: EBA-175 and EBA-140 contain the conserved domain architecture of the EBL family.
source: EBA-175 and EBA-140 contain the conserved domain architecture of the EBL family and bind similarly to GPA and GPC respectively, although the latter binds as a monomer (Malpede and Tolia, 2014; Paing and Tolia, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: EBA-175 and EBA-140 bind similarly to GPA and GPC respectively, although EBA-140 binds as a monomer.
source: EBA-175 and EBA-140 contain the conserved domain architecture of the EBL family and bind similarly to GPA and GPC respectively, although the latter binds as a monomer (Malpede and Tolia, 2014; Paing and Tolia, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The intrinsically disordered EBA-175 III-V domain does not bind erythrocytes.
source: As controls we tested the effect of the intrinsically disordered EBA-175 III-V domain (Blanc et al., 2014), which does not bind erythrocytes (Healer et al., 2013), and it did not significantly influence erythrocyte deformability (p<0.05, Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: EBA-175 III-V domain did not significantly influence erythrocyte deformability (p<0.05).
source: As controls we tested the effect of the intrinsically disordered EBA-175 III-V domain (Blanc et al., 2014), which does not bind erythrocytes (Healer et al., 2013), and it did not significantly influence erythrocyte deformability (p<0.05, Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by AFM data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Erythrocytes incubated with EBA-175 RII together with anti-EBA-175 RII antibodies showed no detectable change in host cell stiffness (p>0.05).
source: Erythrocytes incubated with EBA-175 RII together with anti-EBA-175 RII antibodies, that block binding to GPA and merozoite invasion (Chen et al., 2013; Healer et al., 2013; Sim et al., 2011), showed no detectable change in host cell stiffness (p>0.05) consistent with them blocking ligand binding (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by AFM data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Anti-EBA-175 RII antibodies block binding to GPA and merozoite invasion.
source: Erythrocytes incubated with EBA-175 RII together with anti-EBA-175 RII antibodies, that block binding to GPA and merozoite invasion (Chen et al., 2013; Healer et al., 2013; Sim et al., 2011), showed no detectable change in host cell stiffness (p>0.05) consistent with them blocking ligand binding (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: EBA-175 and EBA-140 binding are both dependent on sialic acid moieties on glycophorin receptors.
source: EBA-175 and EBA-140 binding are both dependent on sialic acid moieties on glycophorin receptors (Adams et al., 2001) and thus sensitive to neuraminidase-treatment of erythrocytes.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: EBA-175 and EBA-140 binding are sensitive to neuraminidase-treatment of erythrocytes.
source: EBA-175 and EBA-140 binding are both dependent on sialic acid moieties on glycophorin receptors (Adams et al., 2001) and thus sensitive to neuraminidase-treatment of erythrocytes.
evidence: This is inferred from the dependence on sialic acid moieties.

claim: EBA-175 RII did not affect the stiffness of neuraminidase-treated erythrocytes.
source: EBA-175 RII did not affect the stiffness of neuraminidase-treated erythrocytes (Figure 1D) indicating a direct link between EBA-175 binding to GPA and changes in erythrocyte deformability.
evidence: This is supported by AFM data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: There is a direct link between EBA-175 binding to GPA and changes in erythrocyte deformability.
source: EBA-175 RII did not affect the stiffness of neuraminidase-treated erythrocytes (Figure 1D) indicating a direct link between EBA-175 binding to GPA and changes in erythrocyte deformability.
evidence: This is inferred from the neuraminidase treatment experiment.

claim: EBA-175 RII binding showed an expected dose response on deformability.
source: EBA-175 RII binding showed an expected dose response on deformability, which was confirmed using ektacytometry (Moyer et al., 2010), consistent with the quantification of EBA-175 RII binding to erythrocytes (Figure 1E; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by AFM and ektacytometry data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Bulk rheology measures of the elongation index showed an increase in erythrocyte deformability with EBA-175 RII reaching a plateau after 35 nM.
source: Bulk rheology measures of the elongation index showed an increase in erythrocyte deformability with EBA-175 RII reaching a plateau after 35 nM (Figure 1E), which was close to saturation of GPA binding sites (Poole, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by rheology data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The plateau in erythrocyte deformability at 35 nM EBA-175 RII was close to saturation of GPA binding sites.
source: Bulk rheology measures of the elongation index showed an increase in erythrocyte deformability with EBA-175 RII reaching a plateau after 35 nM (Figure 1E), which was close to saturation of GPA binding sites (Poole, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by rheology data and a citation about GPA abundance.

claim: Binding of EBA-175 RII to glycophorin A on the erythrocyte surface is responsible for the changes observed in deformability of the host cell.
source: Therefore, binding of EBA-175 RII to glycophorin A on the erythrocyte surface was responsible for the changes observed in deformability of the host cell.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing dose-response and specificity.

claim: An altered intensity of 32P labeling in the EBA-175 RII treated erythrocytes indicated an overall increase of phosphorylation.
source: An altered intensity of 32P labeling in the EBA-175 RII treated erythrocytes indicated an overall increase of phosphorylation, and false-color overlays of aligned autoradiographs showed a shift of particular 2-D spots, revealing some proteins were multiply phosphorylated (Figure 2A and B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by 2D gel autoradiography data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: False-color overlays of aligned autoradiographs showed a shift of particular 2-D spots, revealing some proteins were multiply phosphorylated.
source: An altered intensity of 32P labeling in the EBA-175 RII treated erythrocytes indicated an overall increase of phosphorylation, and false-color overlays of aligned autoradiographs showed a shift of particular 2-D spots, revealing some proteins were multiply phosphorylated (Figure 2A and B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by 2D gel autoradiography data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: LC-MS/MS identified a subset of phosphorylated proteins corresponding to erythrocyte membrane skeleton proteins including tropomodulin-1, adducin-2, tropomyosin, beta-actin, ankyrin-1, protein 4.1 and cofilin-1.
source: Twenty eight of the most prominent 32P-labeled protein spots were excised from an aligned preparative 2-D gel and analyzed by LC-MS/MS. This identified a subset of phosphorylated proteins corresponding to erythrocyte membrane skeleton proteins including tropomodulin-1, adducin-2, tropomyosin, beta-actin, ankyrin-1, protein 4.1 and cofilin-1.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: The identity of phosphorylated proteins was validated by immuno-blot.
source: The identity of these proteins was validated by immuno-blot (Figure 2; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2.

claim: 2-D image analysis of 32P autoradiographs and immuno-blots indicated that 32P labeled 2-D phospho-spots matched accurately with bands for tropomodulin-1 and adducin-2, with clear changes in their phosphorylation state.
source: 2-D image analysis of 32P autoradiographs and immuno-blots of the same membranes indicated that 32P labeled 2-D phospho-spots matched accurately with bands for tropomodulin-1 and adducin-2, with clear changes in their phosphorylation state (Figure 2C–F).
evidence: This is supported by 2D gel and immunoblot data shown in Figure 2C-F.

claim: Global phosphoproteomics analysis revealed a high number (982) of unique phosphopeptides.
source: Global phosphoproteomics analysis of the phosphopeptide enriched Heavy (H) + Light (L) mixture revealed a high number (982) of unique phosphopeptides, and the H/L ratio of unique peptides singly, doubly or triply phosphorylated indicated an overall increase in phosphorylation in the EBA-175 RII treated samples (Figure 2G; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The H/L ratio of unique peptides singly, doubly or triply phosphorylated indicated an overall increase in phosphorylation in the EBA-175 RII treated samples.
source: Global phosphoproteomics analysis of the phosphopeptide enriched Heavy (H) + Light (L) mixture revealed a high number (982) of unique phosphopeptides, and the H/L ratio of unique peptides singly, doubly or triply phosphorylated indicated an overall increase in phosphorylation in the EBA-175 RII treated samples (Figure 2G; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Quantitative LC-MSMS analysis identified approximately 400 erythrocyte phosphoproteins.
source: Quantitative LC-MSMS analysis identified approximately 400 erythrocyte phosphoproteins and revealed a significant (p<0.05) enrichment of phosphopeptides corresponding to trans-membrane spanning glycoproteins and cytoskeletal proteins that include GPA and GPC, adducin, ankyrin and dematin, with many of them multiply phosphorylated (Figure 2H; Figure 2—figure supplement 2; Supplementary file 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Quantitative LC-MSMS analysis revealed a significant (p<0.05) enrichment of phosphopeptides corresponding to trans-membrane spanning glycoproteins and cytoskeletal proteins including GPA and GPC, adducin, ankyrin and dematin, with many of them multiply phosphorylated.
source: Quantitative LC-MSMS analysis identified approximately 400 erythrocyte phosphoproteins and revealed a significant (p<0.05) enrichment of phosphopeptides corresponding to trans-membrane spanning glycoproteins and cytoskeletal proteins that include GPA and GPC, adducin, ankyrin and dematin, with many of them multiply phosphorylated (Figure 2H; Figure 2—figure supplement 2; Supplementary file 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Both GPA and GPC phosphorylation sites were detected in the cytosolic domains of these proteins.
source: Interestingly, both GPA and GPC phosphorylation sites were detected in the cytosolic domains of these proteins (Figure 2I; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: EBA-175 RII binding to erythrocytes induced an overall change in phosphorylation of the cells cytoskeletal proteins.
source: Therefore EBA-175 RII binding to erythrocytes induced an overall change in phosphorylation of the cells cytoskeletal proteins.
evidence: This is inferred from the phosphoproteomics data.

claim: EBA-175 RII binding to erythrocytes suggests an induced modification of the cytoskeleton and consequent increase deformability upon the specific interaction of merozoite ligands with the host erythrocyte.
source: These observations suggested an induced modification of the cytoskeleton and consequent increase deformability upon the specific interaction of merozoite ligands with the host erythrocyte.
evidence: This is inferred from the phosphorylation and deformability data.

claim: TRPM7 is a two-domain protein expressed in most tissues containing both a TRP ion channel and an alpha-kinase domain.
source: TRPM7 is a two-domain protein expressed in most tissues containing both a TRP ion channel and an alpha-kinase domain (Ryazanova et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: TRPM7 phosphorylates tropomodulin-1 at the N-terminal Ser2 and Thr54 residues.
source: TRPM7 phosphorylates tropomodulin-1 at the N- terminal Ser2 and Thr54 residues (Dorovkov et al., 2008), and Ser2 is phosphorylated in erythrocytes (Weber et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Ser2 of tropomodulin-1 is phosphorylated in erythrocytes.
source: TRPM7 phosphorylates tropomodulin-1 at the N- terminal Ser2 and Thr54 residues (Dorovkov et al., 2008), and Ser2 is phosphorylated in erythrocytes (Weber et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: FTY720, waixenicin A and NS8593, which are TRPM7 inhibitors, blocked parasite growth completely.
source: Strikingly, FTY720, waixenicin A and NS8593, which are TRPM7 inhibitors, blocked parasite growth completely.
evidence: This is supported by growth inhibition assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: TRPM7 inhibitors could block parasite growth by impairing invasion.
source: These data along with the phosphorylation of tropomodulin-1, induced by EBA-175 binding to glycophorin A (Figure 2C and D), suggested that TRPM7 may be involved in this phosphorylation cascade and that TRPM7 inhibitors could block parasite growth by impairing invasion.
evidence: This is speculation based on the data.

claim: FTY720 inhibited merozoite invasion (IC50 of 34.1 ± 1.1 µM).
source: FTY720 inhibited merozoite invasion (IC50 of 34.1 ± 1.1 µM) whereas sphingosine had no effect.
evidence: This is supported by invasion inhibition assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Sphingosine had no effect on merozoite invasion.
source: FTY720 inhibited merozoite invasion (IC50 of 34.1 ± 1.1 µM) whereas sphingosine had no effect.
evidence: This is supported by invasion inhibition assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: FTY720 showed potent inhibition of parasite growth (IC50 107.3 ± 1.0 µM).
source: FTY720 (IC50107.3 ± 1.0 µM) showed potent inhibition (Figure 3C) whilst HA1077 and sphingosine showed little to none.
evidence: This is supported by growth inhibition assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: HA1077 and sphingosine showed little to no inhibition of parasite growth.
source: FTY720 (IC50107.3 ± 1.0 µM) showed potent inhibition (Figure 3C) whilst HA1077 and sphingosine showed little to none.
evidence: This is supported by growth inhibition assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Waixenicin A is a slow acting inhibitor of TRPM7.
source: This compound is a slow acting inhibitor of TRPM7 and therefore could be incubated with erythrocytes and washed out before testing merozoite invasion (Zierler et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Waixenicin A-treated erythrocytes showed similar inhibition whether washed (IC50 59.4 ± 1.2 µM) or unwashed (IC50 58.8 ± 1.1 µM).
source: When waixenicin A-treated erythrocytes were tested a similar result was obtained for either washed (IC50 59.4 ± 1.2 µM) or unwashed (IC5058.8 ± 1.1 µM) host cells (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by growth inhibition assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: FTY720 and waixenicin A block invasion of P. falciparum merozoites by inhibiting an essential erythrocyte function(s).
source: Therefore, FTY720 and waixenicin A block invasion of P. falciparum merozoites by inhibiting an essential erythrocyte function(s).
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing inhibition persists after washing.

claim: FTY720 inhibited merozoite invasion of 3D7∆EBA-175 parasites (IC50 20.8 ± 1.2).
source: Interestingly, the same results were observed for 3D7∆EBA-175 parasites that lack expression of EBA-175, where FTY720 inhibited merozoite invasion (IC50 20.8 ± 1.2) (Figure 3B) and parasite growth (IC5095.2 ± 1.0 µM) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by invasion inhibition assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: FTY720 inhibited parasite growth of 3D7∆EBA-175 parasites (IC50 95.2 ± 1.0 µM).
source: Interestingly, the same results were observed for 3D7∆EBA-175 parasites that lack expression of EBA-175, where FTY720 inhibited merozoite invasion (IC50 20.8 ± 1.2) (Figure 3B) and parasite growth (IC5095.2 ± 1.0 µM) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by growth inhibition assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Waixenicin A inhibited 3D7∆EBA-175 growth (IC50 43.8 ± 1.3 µM).
source: Similarly, waixenicin A also inhibited 3D7∆EBA-175 growth (IC50 43.8 ± 1.3 µM) (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by growth inhibition assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The ability of FTY720 and waixenicin A to inhibit invasion of EBA-175 deficient parasites is consistent with this ligand not being essential for merozoite invasion.
